description: Editorial description of the on-screen teaching sequence; not spoken narration. The soundtrack is music.

segments.text: Three additions make attention useful for ordered text: a causal mask, multiple heads and position information.
During next-token training the whole input window is known, but each position must be prevented from looking at its future answer.
Before softmax, put minus infinity above the diagonal of the score matrix. Future positions then receive zero weight.
Bidirectional attention can use the whole input sequence. Causal attention can use the current and preceding positions only.
Multiple heads allow several learned attention patterns to operate in parallel.
With model width 64 and four heads, each head has width 16. Each head’s projections can use all input coordinates.
Two hand-designed heads illustrate different patterns: attending to a previous token or another selected position. Real learned heads need not have these exact roles.
Concatenate the head outputs and apply an output projection to return to the model width.
Without positional information, unrestricted self-attention is permutation equivariant: reordering input tokens reorders their outputs rather than encoding sequence order.
Give positions distinct vectors. Learned positions, sinusoidal positions and rotary methods are alternative designs.
Nearby sinusoidal position vectors can be more similar. The teaching model uses learned position embeddings instead.
A full attention score grid has T×T entries per head. Doubling sequence length makes four times as many scores.
Tiled algorithms such as FlashAttention avoid materializing the full score matrix, reducing memory traffic and storage. They do not remove the quadratic arithmetic of exact full attention.
Pause: width 512 divided among eight heads gives what head width? How much does a score grid grow from 1,000 to 4,000 tokens?
The answers are 64 coordinates per head and sixteen times as many scores.
Recap: mask future positions, combine multiple heads, encode position and account for attention’s memory and compute cost.
